HEADLINE: DDA Is Back On Track And Generating Profit: Lieutenant governor
BODY: The lieutenant governor of Delhi is also chairman of Delhi Development Authority (DDA), the agency that controls land in the city. Since May 2022, when VK Saxena took over as LG, DDA has executed several big projects, including beautification of the city during the G20 summit and redevelopment of the Yamuna floodplain besides undertaking reforms which have redefined its role. Saxena spoke to Atul Mathur and Vibha Sharma on a wide range of issues n You will complete three years as LG next month. What have been the major challenges so far? When I came here, there was a strong desire for change in the city so that the national capital truly looked like one. Despite many challenges which prevented us from accomplishing what we wanted, a lot has been achieved. We wished to bring DDA back on track. The biggest challenge was to prevent the misuse of land and curb encroachments. The floodplain needed to be protected and developed. Being the national capital, Delhi should have top-class infrastructure. It should serve as an example for the entire country. However, that did not happen. DDA only built housing complexes. As a result, planned development did not take place. Ideally, in a national capital region, people should work in the city during the day and return to their homes in NCR towns. The reality is the opposite here. Delhi has essentially become a slum city with predominantly lower-income groups living here and working in NCR. A city should be inclusive, serving all sections — lower class, middle class, upper class and elite. Unfortunately, it favours just one section. This needs to be reversed. n What new projects is DDA taking up now? Quite a few. One is a ‘Gold Souk' project. We have floated the expression of interest and the response has been very positive. ‘Gold Souk' does not mean just gold markets — it will include multiple commercial activities. We have also identified land for sports complexes. The current sports infrastructure in Delhi is outdated with some complexes 25-30 years old. We have approved 50 acres of land each for two sports stadiums in Rohini and Narela. We have already issued expressions of interest for them. Some investors have expressed their desire to develop these into world-class facilities. These stadiums will also have hotels and hostels for athletes, similar to international sports hubs. For athletes, there will be facilities for training, lodging, dining and entertainment. We have also started allocating land for corporate offices and invited expressions of interest. When we organised the G20 summit, we realised there were limited options for good hotels. To address this, we have identified locations in Rohini, Narela and Dwarka for new hotels. This marks the beginning of a new development phase for Delhi. n A major problem in Delhi has been that projects are started and then stretch on and on. Will you insist on deadlines being adhered to? We have imposed strict project timelines. The project must be completed within two-and-a-half years of issuing the letter of award and handing over the land. In extremely rare cases, a six-month extension is allowed. I am confident we will succeed because, so far, all our projects have been completed either on time or earlier. Our officials have now adapted to this work culture, ensuring timely completion. n DDA has made changes in its land policy. What is the objective? Earlier, DDA used to auction land. It will now adopt the long-term lease model. Hotels and sports complexes will be leased for 60 years, ensuring that DDA remains owner of the land. It will help make DDA financially self-sufficient. Despite being the owner of a huge number of properties, DDA's annual rental income was shockingly low — just Rs 150 crore. Our goal is to increase this to Rs 1,000 crore. To put things in perspective, NDMC manages a much smaller area but generates Rs 960 crore in rent. We are working to fix this imbalance. n DDA managed to dispose of a large portion of its housing inventory in the last couple of years. How was it achieved? DDA had around 50,000 unsold flats. We are not going for new construction till the existing inventory is disposed of as maintenance alone was costing crores annually. DDA's previous system restricted buyers — if someone already owned a DDA flat, they couldn't apply again. This was unnecessary. If someone wants to buy multiple flats, why stop them? We also abolished the lottery system which forced people to accept random flats even if they disliked the layout or direction. Now, buyers can choose the flat they want. Income restrictions were another issue – we removed limits that prevented high-income buyers from purchasing flats. The buyers will now be able to merge two flats but ensure the strength of the structure is not affected. These changes have had a massive impact. Another reform was in the booking system. Previously, one could book a flat for just Rs 2,000 and hold it for a year. This allowed brokers to manipulate the inventory. We changed this. The buyers now pay 10% upfront, ensuring only serious buyers participate. These reforms have led to record-breaking sales—DDA sold 8,658 flats, generating Rs 3,353 crore in revenue. In total, we have sold flats worth around Rs 4,500 crore. For the first time in DDA's 65-year history, we generated profit. Last year, DDA had a surplus of Rs 535 crore; this year, we expect it to be around Rs 1,300 crore. n DDA recently organised camps in unauthorised colonies under the PM-UDAY scheme. What has been the response? There were very few takers for the PM Uday Scheme and we have revived it through targeted efforts. We have now established a system. People registering the properties under the scheme now get a leather folder which includes an allotment letter, along with all the receipts of payments made. A copy of the MCD-approved site plan and a copy of the certificate received upon completion of construction are included. This had a significant impact. Through these camps, nearly 45,000 people registered their properties. n Will DDA stop constructing housing complexes now? No, no. That won't happen. The DDA inventory currently has about 30,000 EWS units. In the past two years, it has sold around 18,000 houses. Delhi now needs middle-class and high-end flats which we don't have. DDA doesn't need to construct them. Instead, DDA will supervise after handing over the land to societies. n A large number of flats that remained unsold are in a bad shape. How are you ensuring maintenance of the inventory? Maintenance of the inventory happens regularly. If buildings are not maintained, they deteriorate. That's why we prefer selling them, even at lower rates, to avoid liability. Once occupied, RWAs maintain buildings. Vacant properties need attention. Weeds take over and unauthorised people move in. In Narela, we have hired retired army personnel as guards because thefts were happening. n The commercial complexes built by DDA are not in a good condition. What efforts are you making in this direction? You must have seen how we revamped Nehru Place. We built a walkway, improved parking and cleaned up the messy surroundings. Old buildings need to be renovated every 10 years, but I've noticed that several commercial complexes were built 15 years ago and have been locked up since then or encroached upon. It's difficult to evict such people and renovate the complexes. Some small complexes have 12 to 16 shops with restaurant spaces above. Even in Nehru Place, there's a complex that's been closed. We're auctioning it for a hotel project. We identified several such DDA properties, and if we repurpose them properly, Delhi will shine. n Narela has remained neglected. Can it hope for a revival? To accelerate development of the area, we allotted land to five universities, and of them two have even bought flats for their faculty and students. The project didn't move forward as funds were not issued by the state government last year. Without funds, DDA can't sell the land. The newly-elected govt has restarted the process and we expect the construction work to start soon. n Yamuna was divided into 10 sections for undertaking its cleaning. Five or six sections have already been covered, we believe. Yes, some work has been done. The Yamuna riverfront project is also progressing. Each city's riverfront has a different character. People often compare it with the Sabarmati riverfront but the conditions here are different. In Delhi, certain patches can be developed, not the entire stretch. We have developed areas like Asita, Baansera and Vatika, which are green spaces. Riverfront development doesn't always mean concrete structures; natural green zones are also important. There was flooding in the city earlier but our developed areas did not get damaged. That's the key to sustainable riverfront development. We have successfully developed a 10-acre flower field for the first time in the city. The next phase will be grander. Also, I proposed using the river for recreation and transport of goods. I floated the idea with the then CM Arvind Kejriwal but he paid no heed. DDA is now working on a ropeway project on the river too. The cleaning of a section of Najafgarh drain is also being taken up and it too can be used for transporting goods and saving the city from traffic jams. n What is the status of the land pooling policy aimed at planned development in rural areas as well as MPD 2041? We have submitted the draft MPD 2041 to the Centre and they have to take a call. We are expecting the plan to be notified next month. The land pooling policy will follow. n What is your concept of public art? How are you ensuring that public art installed during the G20 summit and later is properly maintained? We have introduced a number of fountains, sculptures and artefacts at roundabouts and public places in the city. People were questioning us prior to the G 20 event about their maintenance but we are doing the task diligently. The agencies concerned, such as PWD, DDA and NDMC, have been asked to maintain them regularly and ensure these don't become defunct. We are even taking up greenery and beautification work beneath flyovers seriously and had a meeting with the CM recently to decide the action plan for implementing the task. n Do you think charging entrance fees for neighbourhood parks is a good idea? Will this be extended to other places? We are not imposing entrance fees at all parks. These are selected sites which are usually bigger in size and where DDA has made a lot of investment to provide facilities. You won't believe that 1100 tickets are sold in a day at a park in Noida where a nominal fee is charged to ensure these areas are maintained properly and remain secure for visitors. n Now that the govt has changed, what will be your role? My role as Delhi's guardian will continue. I have been a local guardian earlier and will remain so.
--- END ARTICLE ---

HEADLINE: Delhi: Milkman found dead on Heliport road in Rohini
BODY: NEW DELHI: The body of a 35-year-old milkman was found on Heliport road in Rohini area in the national capital, said the Delhi police officials on Monday. The police have registered an FIR. The deceased has been identified as Pradeep who hails from Rithala. The police informed that the information of the presence of a "corpse" was received early in the morning after which the station house officer of the Begumpur police station was rushed to the spot. The milkman along with his motorcycle was found at the spot of the incident. Further investigation into the matter is underway.

--- ARTICLE article_id=81741137 published=2021-03-28 ---
HEADLINE: Gangster who fled from hospital shot dead in Delhi
BODY: NEW DELHI: Within sixty hours of escaping from police custody amid a shootout at GTB Hospital, notorious gangster Kuldeep Maan alias Fajja was killed in another dramatic encounter with cops inside a flat at a housing society in Delhi’s Rohini early Sunday. The special cell got a tipoff on Fajja’s hideout at 9pm Saturday. A crack team of 24 cops, backed by a SWAT squad, reached the society at 1.20am, secured the residents and rang the bell of the flat. The door was opened, police barged in and Fajja started firing. Two cops were hit, but saved by their bulletproof vests. Fajja soon went down and was declared dead in hospital. Fajja opened fire as cops rushed in after ringing the bell thrice Just after escaping from police custody at Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital, Fajja went to a contact, Bhupender Bhuttan, in outer Delhi, collected money and headed towards Rohini according to the directions given to him. Fajja was holed up with his aide Yogender Dahiya for two days at a flat in Tulsi Apartment in Rohini’s Sector 14 and tracking news on his escape, but didn’t use phones or internet, deputy commissioner of police (Special Cell) Pramod Kushwaha claimed. All this while, a team of officers led by ACP Lalit Mohan Negi and Hriday Bhushan from the New Delhi Range of the Special Cell started tracking Fajja and his associates. The cops received a tipoff about Bhuttan and detained him on Saturday evening. It was he who gave police the location of Fajja’s hideout around 9pm. While a surveillance team furtively kept watch at the housing society and the flat since 10pm, the main assault team comprising the two ACPs and inspectors Sunil Rajain and Ravinder Joshi along with 20 others reached the apartment at around 1.20am. The guards at the gate were asked to co-operate and adjacent residents were secured after the presence of “two suspicious men” was confirmed in the flat located on the ground floor. The cops rang the bell thrice — a pre-decided code — of the flat. Once the cops rushed in, Fajja started firing at them from his pistol after taking cover. The cops shot back, and he soon fell on the floor after getting hit. He was taken to Ambedkar hospital and was declared dead on arrival. His postmortem was conducted at the AIIMS and the body handed over to his family on Sunday afternoon. The walls of the flat were riddled with bullets: Fajja fired eight rounds and the cops replied with 12. Dahiya didn’t fire at police and surrendered unhurt the moment the policemen barged in. A pistol was found on him. On March 25, amidst the shootout on the premises of Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital, Delhi Armed Police personnel had shot dead a criminal and injured another after they tried to free Fajja from their custody on Thursday noon. Fajja had been brought to the GTB Hospital for a checkup. Soon after the incident, police officers sealed all border points and alerted patrol to keep watch on suspicious elements. Dozens of raids were conducted at possible hideouts, and criminals outside and inside jails were interrogated for clues. Finally, the breakthrough came on Saturday night. “Fajja was previously involved in 11 criminal cases, including five brutal murders and three cases of armed robberies, extortion and other cases,” DCP Kushwaha said.
--- END ARTICLE ---

--- ARTICLE article_id=107610684 published=2024-02-12 ---
HEADLINE: Inside criminal minds: How these tools are helping Delhi police nail lies
BODY: NEW DELHI: Crimes and criminals in Delhi are prompting investigators to rely increasingly on psychiatric assessment of suspects, something rarely done in the past. Whether it be Shraddha Walkar's murder in south Delhi, Swiss national Nina Berger's killing in west Delhi or even the Parliament security breach cases, police have sought the assistance of forensic psychologists to read the suspects' minds. The trend indicates a changing pattern of people accused of heinous crimes being seemingly normal individuals, requiring the psychology division of Forensic Science Laboratory, Rohini, to assist the cops last year in 130 cases, an increase of about 27% from the previous year. Forensic officials from the Delhi division that TOI spoke to said there were now six units, each headed by a senior psychologist, to cope with the rising number of cases requiring their expertise. "Forensic psychological analysis aims to assist investigators in identifying potentially deceptive individuals and exonerating innocent people," explained a senior official. Many break down during interrogation and confess to their crimes, but there are hardened ones who continually frustrate the law enforcers. They are the ones on whom psychological tests are carried out. In the Shraddha Walkar case, the psychologists wanted to determine why Aaftab Poonawala dismembered her body and dumped them in different locations. They wanted to ascertain what caused so much hatred in his mind to undertake such a gruesome task. Psychological analysis was also important because Aaftab was constantly taking police on wild goose chases using his innate abilities. In the Parliament breach case, the cops wanted to know the mindset that planned and implemented the intrusion into the Lok Sabha. Gurpreet Singh, the alleged killer of Berger, was subjected to tests and the analysis reported signs of "disturbed behaviour". Deepa Verma, director, FSL, said that the primary role of a forensic psychologist begins with understanding and evaluating the mental and emotional state of individuals suspected of committing crimes. Sanjeev Kumar Gupta, division head (crime scene), FSL, said, "The psychologist keeps a close tab on the accused individual's body language and behavioural patterns during test sessions. The focus is on gathering details hidden within their subconscious mind." Another official explained that while suspects might answer some questions without significant physical reactions, some expert-led questions could trigger involuntary responses, such as pupil dilation or uneven leg movement. If the initial tests don't yield the expected results, police can seek court permission for more extensive investigative measures, such as narco-analysis or polygraph tests. In any case, court permission and the suspect's consent are mandatory for any of these procedures. During the narco test, a doctor administers a drug to the suspect in an operation theatre to induce a hypnotic state. Before the tests, the individual is subjected to a series of medical tests to assess his or her health condition. During the hypnotic state, the experts asks questions while recording the entire process. In a polygraph test, instruments such as electrodes and cardio-cuffs are attached to measure heartbeat breathing pattern, etc., when the suspect is made to answer questions related to the crime. In many cases, experts use a layered voice stress analyser to dissect psychological reactions like emotions, stress, uneasiness, energy levels and voice concentration. FSL also has brain fingerprinting instruments that use electro-encephalography (EEG) to map brainwave patterns. This helps investigators determine whether the suspects have knowledge about the crime. There were cases where FSL experts had also handled psychological autopsies. "In an effort to understand the mind of a deceased, a psychological autopsy delves into medical records, interviews friends and family, and gathers information about their mental state before death," the officer explained.
--- END ARTICLE ---
